title: Nine Months on Nasdaq: Why Pets.com Chose an Orderly Wind-Down
dek: In November 2000 the online pet shop's chief executive, Julie Wainwright, closed it while there was still money to hand back, and lived with the ridicule for years.

story.event: Closing the company nine months after its stock-market listing, with cash left to return to shareholders
story.summary: On 7 November 2000 Pets.com, the San Francisco online pet-supply retailer founded by Greg McLemore and run by chief executive Julie Wainwright, announced an orderly wind-down nine months after its February 2000 listing, after failing to find new money or a buyer. It laid off 255 of its 320 staff, sold its assets and aimed to return cash to shareholders; retention bonuses for executives drew criticism, and Wainwright later described the personal cost.
paragraphs: On 7 November 2000 Pets.com, the San Francisco online pet-supply shop known for a wisecracking sock-puppet dog, said it would stop taking orders in two days. It had been a public company for nine months: in February it had sold 7.5 million shares at $11 each on Nasdaq. That day the shares closed at 22 cents.

The business was not Julie Wainwright's idea. Greg McLemore, a Pasadena entrepreneur, had registered the Pets.com address in 1994 and in 1998 spun the shop out of his internet incubator, WebMagic. In early 1999 the venture firm Hummer Winblad invested and handed the running of it to Wainwright, formerly head of the video retailer Reel.com, and she soon brought in Amazon as an investor. By the listing the company had lost $61.8 million on $5.8 million of sales, and its goods cost it more than customers paid.

By the autumn it needed perhaps $20 million to $30 million more. Merrill Lynch approached more than 50 possible buyers or backers; fewer than eight would even visit. In the third quarter Pets.com lost $21.7 million on sales of $9.4 million. Wainwright, chairman as well as chief executive, chose to stop while something could be handed back. "With no better offers and avenues effectively exhausted, we felt that the best option was an orderly wind down," she said. Of 320 staff, 255 were laid off at once.

Filings later showed the board had approved retention bonuses of up to $225,000 for ten executives, Wainwright among them, to see the closure through; some analysts questioned the timing. The company estimated shareholders might eventually receive up to about 25 cents a share, agreed to sell its name to Petsmart.com, and quietly gave more than 21 tons of dog food to Alaskan villages whose sled dogs were going hungry after a salmon collapse.

Wainwright later said closing "made me sick to my stomach", that her husband asked for a divorce that same week, and that afterwards she "wallowed way too long." About a decade later she founded The RealReal.

quote.text: why, my dear Crito, should we care about the opinion of the many? Good men, and they are the only persons who are worth considering, will think of these things truly as they occurred.
quote.source_title: Crito, tr. Benjamin Jowett, Project Gutenberg eBook #1657
quote.connection: Pets.com became a punchline, and for years people laughed at Wainwright. Socrates says the opinion worth weighing belongs to those who look at what actually happened, which here includes both the money kept back for shareholders and the bonuses paid to finish the job.

reflection: Most of what people remember about Pets.com is a sock puppet and a joke. What happened was more ordinary and more human: a board looked at the money left and the offers that never came, and stopped while something could still be returned. Then a woman went home to a very bad week and took years to feel like herself again.

You may be judged at times by people who saw only the headline. It helps to decide in advance whose reading of your work you will take seriously, and to let the rest pass, even when it stings. Recovery can take longer than the event did; that is not a flaw in you.
invitation: Write down the names of two or three people whose judgement of your work you would trust because they would look at what actually happened. Keep the note somewhere you will find it on a hard day.

cross_checks.claim: Pets.com announced its orderly wind-down on 7 November 2000 and laid off 255 of its 320 staff.
Of more than 50 prospects contacted through Merrill Lynch, fewer than eight would even visit.
Greg McLemore founded Pets.com; Julie Wainwright was brought in as chief executive in 1999.
Pets.com listed on Nasdaq in February 2000 at $11 a share, nine months before the closure.
Wainwright's statement: 'With no better offers and avenues effectively exhausted, we felt that the best option was an orderly wind down'.
The shares closed at 22 cents on the day of the announcement.

research_notes: Founder: Pets.com was founded by Greg McLemore (CNET calls him the founder; WebMagic's 1999 note names McLemore and Eva Woodsmall, 1998, as a WebMagic spin-off; Newsweek dates his registration of the domain to 1994). Julie Wainwright was the chief executive brought in by Hummer Winblad in early 1999 (Newsweek, June 1999), so the founder field names McLemore as founder and Wainwright as chief executive, and the story says so. HerMoney's line that she was 'picked to run pets.com in early 2000' conflicts with Newsweek (1999) and CNET (February 2000, already chief executive) and is not used. Share price on 7 November 2000: CNN gives 19 cents in afternoon trade; AP/CBS and Pinsent Masons give a 22-cent close; the story uses the close. IPO proceeds: CNET's headline gives $82.5 million gross, its text about $76 million after expenses; the story gives only the share count and price. Amazon's stake is reported as 50% (Newsweek, 1999), 40.7% before the IPO and 30.4% after (CNET), about 30% (CNN) and 24.5% (Computerworld, December 2000); the story gives no percentage. Tedium dates the announcement to 6 November; contemporary reports give 7 November. Shareholder returns: the only figure from a reliable source is the company's own estimate of up to about $0.25 per share over time (Computerworld from the proxy filing); a widely repeated '17 cents on the dollar' figure comes from unsourced pages and is not used. SEC filings were not consulted directly. Divorce timing: Wainwright told HerMoney her husband asked for a divorce 'that morning'; SmartCompany quotes her writing that it was the day before she announced the shutdown; the story says 'that same week'. The retention bonuses are stated as Computerworld reported them from the 10-Q, with the analysts' doubts attributed to them; no court or regulator found wrongdoing. The PetSmart offer rejected for being below net cash value (Wikipedia, marked citation needed) is not used. The Crito passage is Socrates answering Crito's fear of public opinion before his execution; it is applied here by analogy.
